thread.title: Market Volatility Bulletin: Equities In A Tizzy As Trade Truce Fades

author: The Balance of Trade
title: Market Volatility Bulletin: Equities In A Tizzy As Trade Truce Fades
text:
Market Intro
CNBC: 12:53 PM EST
So much for the pop on the Kum-Ba-Yah cooperation move between China and the US. As it turns out, investors can see further out than ninety days (the length of the suspension in tariffs). Stocks ( SPY , DIA , QQQ , IWM ) are down a good bit in Tuesday trade, though still at about the same level they were last Thursday (i.e., maybe the drop isn't so bad in its present state).
The pain is being felt globally ( ACWX , EFA , EEM ), but the S&P tends to move with a lower beta to world equities, and so I'll argue that the drop is somewhat particular to the S&P here.
Don't blame rates. Treasury yields (i.e. F , TLT , AGG ) are down sharply today, at most tenures. The 2-10 Treasury pair is now only 10 basis points wide…
Spot volatility trades near its long term average, near 20.
Thoughts on Volatility
Awesome line! While an inverted yield curve often does precede a bear market in stocks and/or a recession, it is not 100% accurate as a forecaster of either.
Beyond that, monetary policy over the last decade has been such that we should have significant reason to question whether the signals mean what they have in the historical record. When trillions of dollars of USTs were purchased, many of them rather long-dated, I am suspicious that the yield curve may have otherwise had a very different "natural" state over most of the last decade, and we could only now be getting a better sense as to what that new normal would have looked like: flat, or perhaps even inverted.
Investing should be a process relatively free of emotions. While it's natural, in the right context healthy, and maybe fun, to get into heated debates, we should gratefully take in quality analysis that happens to disagree with our own.
I presume here that is not people who have no direct Apple ( AAPL ) exposure that are taking issue with downgrades. It's okay to have a stance, but you want to do whatever you can in your power to remain objective, especially as facts on the ground change.
This third tweet compliments the prior one rather well. Markets in my experience are rarely interested in what the price "should" do, no matter how soundly constructed one's argument may be.
I tend to be more of a dollar bull, but Santiago Capital does raise some important themes for what arguably should be plaguing the dollar. In my view, a weaker dollar would water down volatility for global assets.
Term Structure
The funny part is that it doesn't matter at all who remits the tax. Economists refer to "incidence" as the relative sharing of a burden (or the removal thereof) between buyer and seller. This tends to be more closely related not to which party writes the check, but rather on the relative price inelasticities of the parties involved (i.e. which party values its counterparty more).
As more of these kinds of thorny issues surface and get treated as credible sources of volatility by market practitioners, it becomes more difficult for measures such as the VIX to hang out at the low end of its recent historical range.
The term structure sure took notice of Tuesday's negative price action. It interests me to see how flexible the VX futures are if VIX snaps around rather wildly.
I think the front end could get choppy, as evidenced by the fact that much of the shape of the previous close took place near the end of Monday's trading session.
The term structure, HV20, and spot VIX are all clustered rather closely to one another. Should HV remain near this level, I have a difficult time thinking that spot VIX or VX futures will veer much from their current position.
VVIX recently touched a three-month low, corresponding to early September when market action looked very different. SPX was near 2900 at that time, and we were seeing vol readings not unlike those of calendar year 2017.
So while spot VIX is printing hot here, I read VVIX as saying that the base case is for more of the same. I read that as some thrashing, and likely not positive for stocks (which is not necessarily the same as downright bad for stocks).
Conclusion If this is your first time reading Market Volatility Bulletin, thanks for giving it a try. If you're a regular, I thank you for your ongoing contributions in the comments section.
Robin makes some strong points in the above comment . For the time being, short vol positions such as SVXY are likely viewed more as trades rather than longer term investments. We saw last week how vol can absolutely take a hit, and the vol shorts performed quite well.
The trouble is the short vol trade isn't getting much traction, and the core factors (roll yield) that made the trade work is not currently in place.
Thank you for reading.
